🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.29% (intraday, 7-year +18bp). At trading day 7 (last close) it was -0.85% against a five-campaign average of -0.13% at the same point — only 2022-23 was worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +20bp since the hike vs a +2bp campaign average at the same point.
  • Stocks: US futures point lower after Monday's gains; Tokyo fell, Europe is rising.
  • FX: The dollar is firmer; the euro is slipping and trading below its recent averages.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq are unusually far above their long-run average prices.
  • Sectors: Tech leads the market; utilities, real estate and materials have lagged this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: The extra yield on company bonds is near historic lows, so little stress.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; higher rates and oil are the main pressure points.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady, but about half of prices still rise over 3%.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip stocks and loose credit look like 2000; overall valuations less so.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron reports Wednesday with a big expected move; Oura's IPO prices this week.
  • Iran: Trump rejected Iran's plan to reopen Hormuz; talks may resume this week.
  • Warsh: Markets see better-than-even odds of another Fed rate hike in October.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral-to-cautious: rising yields and oil threaten stretched stock prices.
  • Trades: Hedge stock gains, favor the dollar over the euro, avoid junk bonds.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 24 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Pre-market: Zero names cleared either rulebook, and honestly the rules got this one right. Watch PPLI (MGM takeover chatter) and BE (Oracle) at the open, but nobody gets a trade from me off stale levels.
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +1.20 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 100th pctile, -0bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Yields at 5.2% and pricier oil test a stretched rally; stay disciplined.

The biggest story this morning is rates. The US 10Y yield is 5.213%, up 5.26bp, and the 2Y is 4.9097%, up 5.81bp. Oil is also rallying: WTI is up 2.01% to 94.27 and Brent is up 1.87% to 106.27 after President Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz (CBS News/Al Jazeera). That combination is weighing on US futures after a solid prior session, when the S&P 500 rose 0.51% to 7743.41, the Dow rose 0.93% and the Nasdaq rose 0.48%. ES futures are down 0.32%, NQ 0.50% and Dow futures 0.47%. Europe is trading positive: the Euro Stoxx 50 is up 0.44% and the FTSE 100 up 0.48%. Tokyo closed lower, with the Nikkei down 0.73%. Precious metals are being hit hard, with gold down 3.20% and silver down 4.85%, which fits a stronger dollar (DXY up 0.21% to 101.188) and higher real yields. The VIX rose 1.15 to 16.02. Sentiment has moved from complacent to cautious. Credit remains calm, but equities are statistically stretched and rates keep grinding higher.

“With the 10-year above 5.2% and Brent above $106, this is a market to stay disciplined in, not one to chase.”

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

US sectors show growth over value and a sharp sell-off in defensives and rate-sensitive groups over the past month. Info Tech leads on every window: 1d +0.99%, 1w +3.11%, 1m +7.3%, YTD +28.28%. Comm Services is also strong on 1m (+4.77%). The losers over 1m are rate-sensitive: Utilities -8.77% (YTD -8.5%), Real Estate -7.19%, Materials -6.69%, Financials -5.64% and Industrials -5.32%. Energy leads YTD (+35.56%) but fell 2.99% over 1w and 0.87% on the day, even with oil rising. Globally the picture is similar: Info Tech is up 35.63% YTD and 3.77% over 1m, while Materials (-7.36%), Real Estate (-6.21%) and Utilities (-5.65%) lead the 1m declines. Leadership is narrow, concentrated in tech and AI. Rising rates are punishing the 'bond proxies' and cyclicals are fading, which is late-cycle concentration rather than broad rotation.

Credit shows complacency, not stress. US IG OAS is 0.80% (z-score -0.8, 6th percentile of history; historical range 0.71% to 6.18%). US HY OAS is 2.94% (z-score -0.79, 13th percentile; +12bp on the day). EUR IG is 0.87% (16th percentile), EUR HY 3.00% (16th percentile) and EM USD 1.64% (4th percentile, z-score -1.34). Against past crises, current levels register 0 on the GFC, EuroDebt and COVID scales. The only non-zero reading is HY at 4 on the 2022 hike scale. Analyst key levels. IG at 0.71% (historical tight) would require oil to calm and yields to peak. A move back through 1.00% would require the 10Y holding above 5.2% alongside an equity drawdown. HY is the tell: 2.33% (historical low) is the upside case, while 3.50% or more would signal that the combination of Fed hikes and oil is biting on leveraged issuers. At these levels there is little spread cushion to absorb a shock.

The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.20 vol points (97th percentile of the 29 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 96.0 (69th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 37bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.21%2026-09-28

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (95bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.21 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Moderately persistent. The core-trend measures (median, trimmed-mean and sticky CPI/PCE) sit in the middle-to-upper part of their history, and most show 'falling' direction, which argues against re-acceleration. However, breadth is uncomfortable: per the Dallas Fed distribution, 52.2% of the PCE basket is inflating above 3% (9.3% above 10%, 13.0% at 5-10%, 29.9% at 3-5%). Core PCE at 3.34% is well above Core CPI's 2.4%, and oil above $94 will feed headline inflation. This is not a spiral, but the Fed has little room to declare victory.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Bubble risk today comes from concentration and the macro backdrop rather than broad valuation. The top 10 stocks are roughly 40% of the S&P 500, versus about 25% in the dot-com era (Motley Fool). The Shiller CAPE is 41.18 and has held above 40 since May, which has happened only once before, ahead of the 2000 crash (GuruFocus/Fool). The Buffett indicator is above 237% (BigGo Finance). The Nasdaq's trailing P/E of 39.02 is nowhere near the dot-com 175x, but semiconductors at 57.67x are close to the 2000-analog 60x. Micron's print this week, with revenue expected to rise more than 350% year over year, tests that group directly. Credit and volatility complacency amplify the downside if rates keep climbing. The 2000 analog peaked 113 months after the Oct-1990 anchor and fell 78% over 31 months, while the current cycle is 47 months past its Oct-2022 anchor. The ipo_froth_pct and lt_eps_growth_pct figures are analyst estimates.

⚔️Iran War

On Saturday President Trump rejected Iran's latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the war, which offered reopening within seven days. He told Axios he expects US negotiators to hold more talks with Iran this week on a different deal (CBS News). Foreign Minister Araghchi said Tehran is still awaiting an official US response and called Trump's comments a 'first reaction' (CBS News). President Pezeshkian told CBS that Iran would allow UN nuclear inspectors in as part of a long-term ceasefire despite an 'atmosphere of distrust'. On Sunday Trump said he has not ruled out more military strikes on Iran before the November midterms (CBS News). Al Jazeera reports the US refuted an Iranian claim to have seized an 'advanced' drone in Hormuz. Market read (analyst inference): the deadlock plus an explicit strike threat explains Brent at 106.27 (+1.87%). A credible reopening would be the single biggest downside catalyst for oil.

Sources: Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week after rejecting proposal - CBS News · Iran war updates: US refutes claim that 'advanced' drone seized in Hormuz - Al Jazeera · Iran war updates: Trump rejects Tehran's proposal to reopen Hormuz - Al Jazeera · Early Edition: September 28, 2026 - Just Security

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

October FOMC: a 25bp hike is slightly more likely than not. Per CME data cited in reports, odds of a hike by October have crossed 50%, and most traders see a quarter-point hike by December. At Jackson Hole Warsh said inflation hasn't meaningfully improved and there is 'work to do' (CNBC/Chase). Inference: with Core PCE at 3.34% and oil above $94, he is unlikely to resist a committee majority.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his record: one to two more 25bp hikes into early 2027, then a hold, combined with continued balance-sheet shrinkage as part of the 'regime change' agenda CNBC describes (meeting internal resistance). Cuts are unlikely within a year unless the labor market breaks. Unemployment is currently 4.1% and payrolls +162k. This is an analyst inference, not guidance.

Warsh's Jackson Hole speech lifted hike odds, and analysts noted it may put the Fed 'at odds' with the Treasury (CNBC, Aug 31). Kiplinger's live coverage reports the FOMC raised the funds rate at the September meeting, the first hike since 2023. CNBC (Sep 25) describes Warsh pushing rapid change to the Fed's framework and balance sheet while meeting resistance. Flag: search summaries gave conflicting accounts of Warsh's personal stance at the September vote, so this read leans on his on-record Jackson Hole comments rather than that quote. The rise in the 2Y (+5.81bp to 4.9097%) today is consistent with the market pricing more hikes.
